blocks.text: Stability-Aware Alignment for Single-Source Domain Generalization in Medical Image Segmentation

Single-source domain generalization (SSDG) for medical image seg- mentation aims to learn a robust model from a single annotated source domain that generalizes well to unseen target domains. Re- cent advances mainly rely on augmentation and invariant represen- tation learning. However, existing methods often impose uniform consistency constraints and implicitly assume that all perturbed regions are equally reliable for alignment. Such uniform alignment may amplify unstable or noisy regions, especially under strong style perturbations, thereby limiting generalization. In this paper, we propose a Stability-Aware Alignment (SAA) method that explicitly models cross-view semantic stability for feature alignment. Specif- ically, we first design a tri-view perturbation scheme to induce diverse shifts and estimate region-wise stability from cross-view consistency. We then introduce a stability-guided region selection mechanism to identify reliable anatomical regions, followed by a distance-weighted alignment strategy that modulates alignment strength according to stability confidence. Furthermore, we incor- porate a structure–style decoupling module to suppress domain- specific appearance variations while preserving task-relevant struc- tural representations. By coupling stability estimation with align- ment regulation, our method avoids over-constraining unstable regions and promotes learning of domain-invariant structural fea- tures. Extensive experiments on cross-modality and cross-sequence medical image segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that SAA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SSDG methods, yielding superior robustness on unseen domains.

Medical image segmentation is fundamental to many clinical ap- plications, including diagnosis, treatment planning, and outcome evaluation. Recently, deep-learning-based methods has achieved remarkable success in this task [12, 33]. However, most methods rely on the assumption that the training and test data are drawn from the same distribution. In practice, medical images acquired across institutions, scanners, and protocols often exhibit substan- tial appearance variations, causing domain shifts that significantly degrade segmentation performance on unseen targets [14, 27, 37]. To mitigate domain shifts, prior studies have explored domain adaptation and multi-source domain generalization [9, 46]. How- ever, access to unlabeled target-domain data or multiple source domains is often impractical in medical scenarios due to privacy, regulatory, and annotation constraints. This makes single-source domain generalization (SSDG), which learns from only one source domain and generalizes to unseen targets, a more realistic yet more challenging setting. The core challenge of SSDG is to bridge the gap between source and unseen target domains. In medical imag- ing, anatomical structure is generally consistent, whereas inten- sity, contrast, texture, and noise may vary substantially across do- mains. These variations are largely style-related rather than label- governing semantics [30, 32]. Therefore, SSDG for medical image segmentation should encourage the model to rely on structure- relevant, domain-stable cues while reducing sensitivity to appear- ance variations and spurious context correlations [30]. This requires not only increasing appearance diversity during training, but also identifying which semantic responses remain reliable when pertur- bations become stronger. Existing SSDG methods for medical image segmentation mainly follow two paradigms: input-level augmentation and representation- level invariant learning [3, 15]. The former increases appearance diversity through style perturbation, saliency-guided augmentation, or frequency-domain manipulation [18, 30, 32, 35], but remains con- strained by source-defined transformations and cannot fully cover unseen target shifts. The latter improves robustness by enforcing consistency across perturbed views or imposing invariant regu- larization in feature space [28, 41, 42]. However, both paradigms largely overlook a critical question: which semantic responses re- main stable under perturbation, and which do not? In practice, perturbations often induce unstable boundary responses and fluc- tuating contextual activations. As a result, indiscriminate global alignment may mix reliable anatomical cues with unstable signals and propagate noise into representation learning, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Moreover, different spatial regions do not contribute equally to robust generalization: anatomically meaningful regions are typi- cally more task-relevant, whereas background or non-interest re- gions may contain domain-specific cues that encourage shortcut learning [21, 45, 48]. Recent attempts to reweight alignment by un- certainty or foreground priors partially alleviate this issue [38, 45].

In this paper, we define semantic stability as the repeatability of representations or predictions for a semantic region under di- verse perturbations. Based on this view, we propose Stability-Aware Alignment (SAA), which explicitly models cross-view semantic sta- bility to guide selective alignment. Specifically, SAA is built upon tri-view perturbation, channel-wise structure-style decoupling, and stability-aware selective alignment. These designs estimate stability across complementary perturbed views, select reliable regions for alignment, and adaptively modulate alignment strength according to semantic consistency. Meanwhile, a channel-wise structure-style decoupling module further suppresses appearance-sensitive chan- nels and improves the reliability of stability modeling. Extensive experiments on cross-modality and cross-sequence benchmarks demonstrate that SAA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SSDG methods. The main contributions of this work are summa- rized as follows:

• We propose SAA, a stability-aware framework for SSDG in medical image segmentation that explicitly models cross- view semantic stability. • We design a selective alignment mechanism that estimates semantic stability to determine where and how strongly alignment should be enforced. • We introduce a channel-wise structure–style decoupling module to suppress appearance-sensitive channels and im- prove stability-aware representation learning. • Extensive experiments on cross-modality and cross-sequence benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
2 Related Works 2.1 Single-Source Domain Generalization for Medical Image Segmentation

Domain generalization for medical image segmentation aims to en- sure robust performance under acquisition-induced shifts without access to target-domain data, and is often further constrained to the single-source regime due to privacy and annotation costs [46]. Re- cent SSDG approaches mainly follow two paradigms: (i) augmentation- driven domain expansion and (ii) domain-invariant feature learn- ing [15, 28]. The first paradigm expands the source distribution via diverse appearance variations. Representative strategies in- clude saliency-guided perturbations [35], frequency-based manip- ulations [19, 32, 49], input-space interpolation [44], and causal or shortcut-breaking perturbations [30]. Other Fourier-based style diversification modules, such as MoreStyle [49], further relax fre- quency constraints to generate richer appearance variations. While effective at increasing input diversity, these approaches remain lim- ited to source-defined transformations and may distort structural semantics [23, 35, 42]. The second paradigm promotes invariance in the prediction or feature space by reducing sensitivity to domain- specific appearance factors. Representative examples include cross- view consistency in IRLSG [28], channel- or style-disentanglement methods, as in C2SDG and ICRN[5, 10], multi-receptive-field fea- ture disentanglement in MRFFD [41], and invariant-representation learning in EIR-SDG through texture–style diversification, adap- tive whitening, and semantic relationship optimization [29]. More recent studies further combine augmentation with explicit rep- resentation constraints, as seen in FSDA-DG and DCON [38, 45]. Overall, recent robust segmentation research increasingly combines multi-view perturbations with representation alignment [26, 34], reflecting a shift toward learning stable, domain-invariant represen- tations rather than relying solely on input diversification [8, 24].
2.2 Multi-view Consistency and Reliability Aware Supervision

A key challenge in invariance learning is that consistency is only as reliable as its supervisory signal. Many methods enforce agreement across perturbed views in prediction or feature space [48], yet noisy predictions or perturbed responses can be amplified under strong perturbations or domain shifts [1, 2, 10]. Such noise amplification ef- fects are well-documented in teacher–student and pseudo-labeling frameworks, where indiscriminate consistency can lead to confir- mation bias [20, 36, 40]. Existing efforts mainly address this issue in three ways. Some improve target quality directly, for example by constructing denoised semantic supervision from synthetic seman- tic stacks [31]. Others modulate consistency using reliability proxies such as uncertainty, entropy, or confidence [7, 25, 47]; representa- tive examples include uncertainty-weighted consistency in FSDA- DG and related uncertainty-aware weighting schemes [39, 45]. A third line of work restricts consistency to informative spatial re- gions, such as object-centric foreground areas in DCON [38] or ambiguous and boundary-related regions in MPDC [51], rather than the full image [22]. Despite these advances, two limitations remain. First, existing methods mainly rely on prediction-based reliability estimates rather

4.1.1 Datasets. We evaluate SAA on two public medical image SSDG benchmarks, covering abdominal cross-modality transfer and cardiac cross-sequence transfer, under the strict single-source setting. The abdominal benchmark is constructed from BTCV CT and CHAOS T2-weighted MRI data [13, 16], while the cardiac bench- mark is based on the MS-CMRSeg dataset [52]. For each benchmark, one modality or sequence is used as the only source domain for training, and the other is used only for testing.

4.1.2 Implementation Details. We adopt a standard U-Net as the segmentation backbone in all experiments, the same as CGSD [30]. The segmentation model is trained with the Adam optimizer. All models are trained from scratch with an initial learning rate of 5 × 10−4 linearly decayed to zero and a batch size of 20. We train for 1500 epochs on the abdominal benchmark and 1800 epochs on the cardiac benchmark on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU with 24 GB memory.

4.1.3 Comparison Methods. We compare SAA with representative baselines under the strict single-source setting, including generic augmentation-based DG methods (Cutout [6], MixStyle [50], Ad- vBias [4], and RandConv[43]), a feature-regularization baseline (RSC [11]), and recent SSDG methods (CSDG [30], SLAug [35], S2S2 [31], and DCON [38]), together with the ERM baseline. All methods use the same backbone, data split, and optimization proto- col for fair comparison.

Table 1 reports the Dice scores on all four SSDG tasks. SAA achieves the best average Dice on all tasks, outperforming ERM, generic DG baselines, and recent SSDG methods, which indicates stronger robustness under both cross-modality and cross-sequence shifts.

4.2.1 Comparisons on Abdominal (BTCV–CHAOS). On the abdomi- nal benchmark, SAA achieves the best average Dice on both MRI→CT and CT→MRI. Compared with ERM, SAA improves the average Dice by 22.57 points on MRI→CT (85.55 vs. 62.98) and by 11.94 points on CT→MRI (89.20 vs. 77.26). Compared with the strongest augmentation baseline RandConv, the gains are 8.99 and 8.54 points, respectively; compared with the feature-regularization baseline RSC, the gains are 19.48 and 15.11 points. Against recent SSDG methods, SAA further surpasses the best competitor by 1.10 points on MRI→CT (vs. DCON) and 0.57 points on CT→MRI (vs. SLAug). Notably, SAA achieves the best scores for all abdominal organs in both transfer directions, indicating consistent improvements rather than gains concentrated on a single structure. The advantage is particularly clear on the harder MRI→CT task, where large ap- pearance discrepancies make purely augmentation-based coverage insufficient. These results show that simply increasing appearance diversity or applying global feature regularization is insufficient under severe cross-modality shifts. By explicitly estimating cross- view stability and restricting alignment to reliable regions, SAA produces more robust anatomical representations.

4.2.2 Comparisons on Cardiac (MS-CMRSeg). On the cardiac bench- mark, SAA also achieves the best average Dice on both LGE→bSSFP and bSSFP→LGE. Compared with ERM, SAA improves the average Dice by 2.64 points on LGE→bSSFP (88.12 vs. 85.48) and by 11.43 points on bSSFP→LGE (87.33 vs. 75.90). Compared with RandConv, the gains are 0.88 and 3.60 points, and compared with RSC, the gains are 2.52 and 9.82 points, respectively. SAA further improves over the strongest recent SSDG baseline by 0.06 points on LGE→bSSFP (vs. DCON) and 0.64 points on bSSFP→LGE (vs. SLAug), while also achieving the best MYO and RVC scores on bSSFP→LGE. On LGE→bSSFP, the margin in average Dice is smaller, but SAA still ranks first overall, showing that the proposed selective alignment re- mains beneficial even when competing methods are already strong. On bSSFP→LGE, the larger gain suggests that SAA is more effec- tive when the target-domain appearance is more challenging and local responses become less reliable. These results suggest that SAA is especially beneficial when local appearance variation is strong and anatomical boundaries are ambiguous, since stability-aware selective alignment helps suppress unreliable responses while pre- serving shape-consistent cues.

We further analyze SAA through component ablation 4.3.1, SAAM core ablation 4.3.2, tri-view validation 4.3.3, hyper-parameter sen- sitivity 4.3.4, and mechanism verification 4.3.5 under the same training protocol as the full model.

4.3.1 Component Ablation. Tables 2 and 3 report the component ablation results on all four SSDG tasks. All three modules improve over the baseline, with SAAM consistently giving the largest gain among the single-module variants, while the Full model achieves the best performance in every task. Specifically, the Full model improves the average Dice from 82.77 to 85.55 on MRI→CT (+2.78), from 86.54 to 88.12 on LGE→bSSFP (+1.58), from 87.24 to 89.20 on CT→MRI (+1.96), and from 85.55 to 87.33 on bSSFP→LGE (+1.78). In comparison, SAAM alone al- ready yields strong gains of +1.92, +1.18, +1.17, and +1.21 on the four tasks, respectively. These results indicate that SAAM is the strongest individual contributor, while RCCS and CGSD provide further complementary improvements in the full model.

4.3.2 SAAM Core Ablation. To isolate the effect of each SAAM component, we remove the alignment term, the stable-region se- lector Ω, or the distance-aware weighting 𝑊while keeping the remaining parts unchanged. As shown in Tables 4 and 5, all three variants underperform the full model on both task-level and organ- level results. At the task level, removing the alignment term reduces the overall Dice from 87.55 to 86.30, while removing Ω and𝑊leads to smaller drops to 86.70 and 86.98, respectively. The same trend is observed on MRI→CT and LGE→bSSFP, where the full model achieves the best average Dice of 85.55 and 88.12. 4.3.3 Effectiveness of Tri-view. Fig. 5 evaluates the tri-view de- sign with CGSD and SAAM fixed. The full configuration (A+B+S) achieves the best performance, while both A+B and A+S outper- form the anchor-only setting. Removing either its local component (S-w/o-L) or texture component (S-w/o-T) degrades performance, showing that effective strong perturbation requires joint modeling of local semantics and texture. To ana- lyze how SAA affects cross-view consistency learning, we visualize the predictions from different views, the stability map 𝑊, the se- lected stable region Ω, and the final alignment weight 𝐴under anchor, base, and strong perturbations. As shown in Fig. 6, the baseline exhibits larger inter-view prediction variation, while our method produces more consistent predictions across perturbed views. This difference is reflected not only in the contour overlap

More importantly, the advantage comes from how SAAM converts estimated stability into compact stable-core selection and foreground-constrained align- ment weights. Instead of enforcing equally strong consistency over all foreground responses, SAAM concentrates alignment on more reliable organ-centered regions. It suppresses overly aggressive alignment on boundary-blurred, locally conflicting, or perturbation- sensitive locations.

In this work, we revisit the fundamental assumption underlying single-source domain generalization for medical image segmen- tation. While most existing approaches implicitly rely on strong augmentations and enforce invariance across all perturbed views, our findings highlight a critical limitation of this paradigm. Medical image augmentations are not always safe. Due to the low contrast, subtle inter-class differences, and anatomical sensitivity inherent to medical images, certain perturbations may selectively distort se- mantically critical regions. Treating all perturbed views as equally reliable and enforcing unconditional invariance can therefore lead to erroneous alignment and compromised generalization. Instead, we demonstrate that effective generalization under single-source constraints depends on identifying which semantic information re- mains stable across different views and aligning only these reliable components. By shifting the focus from unconditional invariance to stability-aware alignment, our work offers a principled perspective on how transferable representations should be learned for medical image segmentation. We hope this perspective encourages future research to reconsider the role of data augmentation and consis- tency constraints in medical image analysis, and to move toward reliability-aware and stability-aware generalization strategies.

Single-source domain generalization (SSDG) for medical image seg- mentation aims to learn a robust model from a single annotated source domain that generalizes well to unseen target domains. Re- cent advances mainly rely on augmentation and invariant represen- tation learning. However, existing methods often impose uniform consistency constraints and implicitly assume that all perturbed regions are equally reliable for alignment. Such uniform alignment may amplify unstable or noisy regions, especially under strong style perturbations, thereby limiting generalization. In this paper, we propose a Stability-Aware Alignment (SAA) method that explicitly models cross-view semantic stability for feature alignment. Specif- ically, we first design a tri-view perturbation scheme to induce diverse shifts and estimate region-wise stability from cross-view consistency. We then introduce a stability-guided region selection mechanism to identify reliable anatomical regions, followed by a distance-weighted alignment strategy that modulates alignment strength according to stability confidence. Furthermore, we incor- porate a structure–style decoupling module to suppress domain- specific appearance variations while preserving task-relevant struc- tural representations. By coupling stability estimation with align- ment regulation, our method avoids over-constraining unstable regions and promotes learning of domain-invariant structural fea- tures. Extensive experiments on cross-modality and cross-sequence medical image segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that SAA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SSDG methods, yielding superior robustness on unseen domains.

Medical image segmentation is fundamental to many clinical ap- plications, including diagnosis, treatment planning, and outcome evaluation. Recently, deep-learning-based methods has achieved remarkable success in this task [12, 33]. However, most methods rely on the assumption that the training and test data are drawn from the same distribution. In practice, medical images acquired across institutions, scanners, and protocols often exhibit substan- tial appearance variations, causing domain shifts that significantly degrade segmentation performance on unseen targets [14, 27, 37]. To mitigate domain shifts, prior studies have explored domain adaptation and multi-source domain generalization [9, 46]. How- ever, access to unlabeled target-domain data or multiple source domains is often impractical in medical scenarios due to privacy, regulatory, and annotation constraints. This makes single-source domain generalization (SSDG), which learns from only one source domain and generalizes to unseen targets, a more realistic yet more challenging setting. The core challenge of SSDG is to bridge the gap between source and unseen target domains. In medical imag- ing, anatomical structure is generally consistent, whereas inten- sity, contrast, texture, and noise may vary substantially across do- mains. These variations are largely style-related rather than label- governing semantics [30, 32]. Therefore, SSDG for medical image segmentation should encourage the model to rely on structure- relevant, domain-stable cues while reducing sensitivity to appear- ance variations and spurious context correlations [30]. This requires not only increasing appearance diversity during training, but also identifying which semantic responses remain reliable when pertur- bations become stronger. Existing SSDG methods for medical image segmentation mainly follow two paradigms: input-level augmentation and representation- level invariant learning [3, 15]. The former increases appearance diversity through style perturbation, saliency-guided augmentation, or frequency-domain manipulation [18, 30, 32, 35], but remains con- strained by source-defined transformations and cannot fully cover unseen target shifts. The latter improves robustness by enforcing consistency across perturbed views or imposing invariant regu- larization in feature space [28, 41, 42]. However, both paradigms largely overlook a critical question: which semantic responses re- main stable under perturbation, and which do not? In practice, perturbations often induce unstable boundary responses and fluc- tuating contextual activations. As a result, indiscriminate global alignment may mix reliable anatomical cues with unstable signals and propagate noise into representation learning, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Moreover, different spatial regions do not contribute equally to robust generalization: anatomically meaningful regions are typi- cally more task-relevant, whereas background or non-interest re- gions may contain domain-specific cues that encourage shortcut learning [21, 45, 48]. Recent attempts to reweight alignment by un- certainty or foreground priors partially alleviate this issue [38, 45].

In this paper, we define semantic stability as the repeatability of representations or predictions for a semantic region under di- verse perturbations. Based on this view, we propose Stability-Aware Alignment (SAA), which explicitly models cross-view semantic sta- bility to guide selective alignment. Specifically, SAA is built upon tri-view perturbation, channel-wise structure-style decoupling, and stability-aware selective alignment. These designs estimate stability across complementary perturbed views, select reliable regions for alignment, and adaptively modulate alignment strength according to semantic consistency. Meanwhile, a channel-wise structure-style decoupling module further suppresses appearance-sensitive chan- nels and improves the reliability of stability modeling. Extensive experiments on cross-modality and cross-sequence benchmarks demonstrate that SAA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SSDG methods. The main contributions of this work are summa- rized as follows:

• We propose SAA, a stability-aware framework for SSDG in medical image segmentation that explicitly models cross- view semantic stability. • We design a selective alignment mechanism that estimates semantic stability to determine where and how strongly alignment should be enforced. • We introduce a channel-wise structure–style decoupling module to suppress appearance-sensitive channels and im- prove stability-aware representation learning. • Extensive experiments on cross-modality and cross-sequence benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
2 Related Works 2.1 Single-Source Domain Generalization for Medical Image Segmentation

Domain generalization for medical image segmentation aims to en- sure robust performance under acquisition-induced shifts without access to target-domain data, and is often further constrained to the single-source regime due to privacy and annotation costs [46]. Re- cent SSDG approaches mainly follow two paradigms: (i) augmentation- driven domain expansion and (ii) domain-invariant feature learn- ing [15, 28]. The first paradigm expands the source distribution via diverse appearance variations. Representative strategies in- clude saliency-guided perturbations [35], frequency-based manip- ulations [19, 32, 49], input-space interpolation [44], and causal or shortcut-breaking perturbations [30]. Other Fourier-based style diversification modules, such as MoreStyle [49], further relax fre- quency constraints to generate richer appearance variations. While effective at increasing input diversity, these approaches remain lim- ited to source-defined transformations and may distort structural semantics [23, 35, 42]. The second paradigm promotes invariance in the prediction or feature space by reducing sensitivity to domain- specific appearance factors. Representative examples include cross- view consistency in IRLSG [28], channel- or style-disentanglement methods, as in C2SDG and ICRN[5, 10], multi-receptive-field fea- ture disentanglement in MRFFD [41], and invariant-representation learning in EIR-SDG through texture–style diversification, adap- tive whitening, and semantic relationship optimization [29]. More recent studies further combine augmentation with explicit rep- resentation constraints, as seen in FSDA-DG and DCON [38, 45]. Overall, recent robust segmentation research increasingly combines multi-view perturbations with representation alignment [26, 34], reflecting a shift toward learning stable, domain-invariant represen- tations rather than relying solely on input diversification [8, 24].
2.2 Multi-view Consistency and Reliability Aware Supervision

A key challenge in invariance learning is that consistency is only as reliable as its supervisory signal. Many methods enforce agreement across perturbed views in prediction or feature space [48], yet noisy predictions or perturbed responses can be amplified under strong perturbations or domain shifts [1, 2, 10]. Such noise amplification ef- fects are well-documented in teacher–student and pseudo-labeling frameworks, where indiscriminate consistency can lead to confir- mation bias [20, 36, 40]. Existing efforts mainly address this issue in three ways. Some improve target quality directly, for example by constructing denoised semantic supervision from synthetic seman- tic stacks [31]. Others modulate consistency using reliability proxies such as uncertainty, entropy, or confidence [7, 25, 47]; representa- tive examples include uncertainty-weighted consistency in FSDA- DG and related uncertainty-aware weighting schemes [39, 45]. A third line of work restricts consistency to informative spatial re- gions, such as object-centric foreground areas in DCON [38] or ambiguous and boundary-related regions in MPDC [51], rather than the full image [22]. 4.1.1 Datasets. We evaluate SAA on two public medical image SSDG benchmarks, covering abdominal cross-modality transfer and cardiac cross-sequence transfer, under the strict single-source setting. The abdominal benchmark is constructed from BTCV CT and CHAOS T2-weighted MRI data [13, 16], while the cardiac bench- mark is based on the MS-CMRSeg dataset [52]. For each benchmark, one modality or sequence is used as the only source domain for training, and the other is used only for testing.

4.1.2 Implementation Details. We adopt a standard U-Net as the segmentation backbone in all experiments, the same as CGSD [30]. The segmentation model is trained with the Adam optimizer. All models are trained from scratch with an initial learning rate of 5 × 10−4 linearly decayed to zero and a batch size of 20. We train for 1500 epochs on the abdominal benchmark and 1800 epochs on the cardiac benchmark on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU with 24 GB memory.

4.1.3 Comparison Methods. We compare SAA with representative baselines under the strict single-source setting, including generic augmentation-based DG methods (Cutout [6], MixStyle [50], Ad- vBias [4], and RandConv[43]), a feature-regularization baseline (RSC [11]), and recent SSDG methods (CSDG [30], SLAug [35], S2S2 [31], and DCON [38]), together with the ERM baseline. All methods use the same backbone, data split, and optimization proto- col for fair comparison.

Table 1 reports the Dice scores on all four SSDG tasks. SAA achieves the best average Dice on all tasks, outperforming ERM, generic DG baselines, and recent SSDG methods, which indicates stronger robustness under both cross-modality and cross-sequence shifts.

4.2.1 Comparisons on Abdominal (BTCV–CHAOS). On the abdomi- nal benchmark, SAA achieves the best average Dice on both MRI→CT and CT→MRI. Compared with ERM, SAA improves the average Dice by 22.57 points on MRI→CT (85.55 vs. 62.98) and by 11.94 points on CT→MRI (89.20 vs. 77.26). Compared with the strongest augmentation baseline RandConv, the gains are 8.99 and 8.54 points, respectively; compared with the feature-regularization baseline RSC, the gains are 19.48 and 15.11 points. Against recent SSDG methods, SAA further surpasses the best competitor by 1.10 points on MRI→CT (vs. DCON) and 0.57 points on CT→MRI (vs. SLAug). Notably, SAA achieves the best scores for all abdominal organs in both transfer directions, indicating consistent improvements rather than gains concentrated on a single structure. The advantage is particularly clear on the harder MRI→CT task, where large ap- pearance discrepancies make purely augmentation-based coverage insufficient. These results show that simply increasing appearance diversity or applying global feature regularization is insufficient under severe cross-modality shifts. By explicitly estimating cross- view stability and restricting alignment to reliable regions, SAA produces more robust anatomical representations.

4.2.2 Comparisons on Cardiac (MS-CMRSeg). On the cardiac bench- mark, SAA also achieves the best average Dice on both LGE→bSSFP and bSSFP→LGE. As shown in Fig. 6, the baseline exhibits larger inter-view prediction variation, while our method produces more consistent predictions across perturbed views. This difference is reflected not only in the contour overlap

More importantly, the advantage comes from how SAAM converts estimated stability into compact stable-core selection and foreground-constrained align- ment weights. Instead of enforcing equally strong consistency over all foreground responses, SAAM concentrates alignment on more reliable organ-centered regions. It suppresses overly aggressive alignment on boundary-blurred, locally conflicting, or perturbation- sensitive locations.

In this work, we revisit the fundamental assumption underlying single-source domain generalization for medical image segmen- tation. While most existing approaches implicitly rely on strong augmentations and enforce invariance across all perturbed views, our findings highlight a critical limitation of this paradigm. Medical image augmentations are not always safe. Due to the low contrast, subtle inter-class differences, and anatomical sensitivity inherent to medical images, certain perturbations may selectively distort se- mantically critical regions. Treating all perturbed views as equally reliable and enforcing unconditional invariance can therefore lead to erroneous alignment and compromised generalization. Instead, we demonstrate that effective generalization under single-source constraints depends on identifying which semantic information re- mains stable across different views and aligning only these reliable components. By shifting the focus from unconditional invariance to stability-aware alignment, our work offers a principled perspective on how transferable representations should be learned for medical image segmentation. We hope this perspective encourages future research to reconsider the role of data augmentation and consis- tency constraints in medical image analysis, and to move toward reliability-aware and stability-aware generalization strategies.
